Reproductive biology of the Ocellated wrasse Symphodus ocellatus has been studied in the coastal waters of the Mediterranean Sea, where individuals build intricate nests of algae and seagrass. Field surveys indicate that males construct and defend these nests during the spawning season, actively guarding the fertilised eggs until eclosion occurs. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches a mean value of 12% [GSI = 12%] when water temperatures are at approximately 18.9 °C [T = 18.9 °C]. Nest-guarding males display a characteristic coloration and aggressively chase intruders, a behaviour that imposes substantial energetic costs. Available data suggest that the onset of sexual maturity is tied to the attainment of a specific body size, a pattern common among labrid fishes. The wet weight at puberty is estimated at 0.87 grams [Wwp = 0.87 grams], a mass that marks the transition to reproductive competence in both sexes. Below this threshold, individuals are typically observed as non-territorial juveniles foraging in seagrass meadows.

Growth and size at key life stages provide important insights into the life history strategy of Symphodus ocellatus. The total length at puberty, which is the size at which individuals first become capable of reproducing, has been recorded at 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters]. This is a relatively small body size compared to many other Mediterranean wrasses, implying a comparatively fast life pace. The ultimate total length, representing the maximum size an individual can attain, is 18.5 centimeters [Li = 18.5 centimeters], a value consistent with the species' position as a medium-sized member of the genus. Mature adults of this length are frequently observed guarding nests in shallow rocky habitats. The length-mass relationship for this species, derived from morphometric measurements of field-caught specimens, allows for estimation of body mass at different sizes. Consequently, the ultimate wet weight, which is the maximum body mass reached by fully grown adults, is approximately 99 grams [Wwi = approximately 99 grams]. This mass reflects the energetic ceiling for somatic growth under typical resource availability in the western Mediterranean. The asymptotic mass of 99 grams is consistent with the territorial and nest-guarding lifestyle, where males must allocate energy to both body maintenance and reproductive effort.

The early life stages of the Ocellated wrasse are characterised by a pelagic larval phase that follows egg hatching. Fertilised ova are demersal and adhesive, deposited by the female within the nest structure, where the male provides exclusive paternal care until the yolk-sac larva emerges. Data extrapolated from measurements of a congeneric species, Labrus bergylta, provide estimates for initial masses. The wet weight at birth, which corresponds to the mass of the newly hatched prolarva immediately after eclosion, is roughly 0.000195 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.000195 grams]. This extremely small size is typical of labrids that produce numerous small eggs, a strategy favouring high fecundity at the expense of per-offspring investment. The yolk-sac is rapidly absorbed over the first few days post-hatching, after which the larvae must locate suitable planktonic prey. The transition from endogenous to exogenous nutrition marks a critical bottleneck, and larval mortality during this exotrophic transition is presumed to be high in the wild.

Longevity and the timing of life history events are influenced strongly by the thermal environment. The maximum lifespan documented for the Ocellated wrasse is 5 years [am = 5 years] when maintained at a water temperature of 18.9 °C [T = 18.9 °C], a value that was recorded from a long-term mark-recapture study in a protected coastal lagoon. This lifespan is moderate among small-bodied labrids, reflecting a trade-off between early reproduction and extended survival. Individuals that survive the pelagic larval phase and successfully recruit to the benthic habitat as post-metamorphic juveniles face an array of predatory risks, including those from larger piscivorous fish. The age structure of the population suggests that mortality is high during the first year of life, with a marked decrease thereafter. Field observations indicate that some individuals may reach the upper limit of this lifespan, but such cases are relatively uncommon, likely due to the energetic demands of repeated annual spawning seasons. In comparison to other Mediterranean labrids of similar body size, the 5-year lifespan is relatively typical, though some congeners have been reported to live up to 8 years in cooler waters.

The relationship between body size and reproductive output is a central theme in the life history of this fish. The wet weight at puberty, recorded at 0.87 grams [Wwp = 0.87 grams], represents the mass at which the gonads become active and males begin to establish nesting territories. This mass is reached at a total length of 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters], which confirms the early maturation strategy of the species. In comparative terms, the ultimate total length of 18.5 centimeters [Li = 18.5 centimeters] is achieved by relatively few individuals, and the corresponding ultimate wet weight of 99 grams [Wwi = 99 grams] is approached asymptotically. The shape of the growth curve suggests that energy is increasingly channelled into reproduction rather than somatic growth after the onset of maturity. The gonadosomatic index of 12% [GSI = 12%] was measured at 18.9 °C [T = 18.9 °C].
